claims.text: The identity of X in CrFeCoNiX controls the nature of the high-temperature protective oxide through changes in oxide-scale chemistry and diffusion.
Si addition promotes formation of a dense mixed Si-Cr oxide.
The Si-promoted mixed oxide grows slowly and remains coherent.
The Si-promoted oxide accommodates thermal expansion and minimizes internal stress.
Mn- or Al-containing variants form phase-segregated oxide scales with higher interfacial stresses.
The phase segregation and interfacial stresses in Mn- or Al-containing scales promote cracking and spallation above 900 °C.
Arc melting followed by homogenizing heat treatment ensures a uniform solid-solution microstructure in the tested alloys.
The proposed comparison varies X among Si, Mn, and Al while holding alloy processing and oxidation exposure constant.
The decisive structural mediator is oxide-scale composition, phase homogeneity, continuity, and mechanical integrity.
Element-specific oxidation kinetics and diffusion behavior determine oxide composition and interfacial bonding.
Si slows oxide growth and promotes a viscous, glassy mixed oxide.
The proposed glassy Si-containing oxide bridges grain boundaries and accommodates thermal strain.
Mn and Al cause faster oxide growth and oxide-phase separation, producing brittle, crack-prone scales.
At 950 °C for 200 hours, the Si-containing alloy will form a thinner, more coherent, slower-growing, and more adherent scale than the Mn- and Al-containing variants.
The Mn- and Al-containing variants will develop thicker, less uniform scales with more cracking and spallation.
CrFeCoNi without X, or with an unspecified neutral X, is expected to form a less protective scale than the Si-containing alloy.
Minor inhomogeneities or impurities may alter oxide growth rates and cracking thresholds.
